summary: 39b covers: the 'chamtzan' era after Shimon HaTzaddik's death; the year he died and its signs (thin Azazel goat, red thread stayed red); placement of the lots on the goats' heads with the designation formula 'chattat l'HaShem'; baraita about the God-lot historically coming up right; R. Yannai's dispute about whether the right-hand position is halachically required.

learning.ahaMoment: Chamtzan = the bitterness of decline; the sweetness of Shimon HaTzaddik's era contrasted with what came after.
learning.memoryAnchor: Sweet era (Shimon) vs sour era (aftermath) - one word captures the contrast.
learning.learnerQuestion: What does the term 'chamtzan' (sour/bitter) capture about the period immediately following Shimon HaTzaddik's death?
learning.coreTension: The four-miracle era was sweet (good); chamtzan names what came after as its opposite, but the single word leaves open how sharply or how soon the change occurred.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara's placement of 'chamtzan' directly after the account of the signs ceasing ties the word to that same abrupt transition, not a gradual fading.

takeaway.text: 'Chamtzan' (sour, bitter) names the era after Shimon HaTzaddik's death, when the four miraculous signs of his service ceased, the word captures a sudden reversal, not a slow decline.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may assume 'chamtzan' implies a gradual souring over generations, missing that the Gemara places it immediately after the account of the signs reversing at his death.

misconceptions.misconception: The era after Shimon HaTzaddik began a gradual decline that slowly worsened over generations.
misconceptions.correction: The decline was immediate - the very next year after his death the pattern changed. 'Chamtzan' describes a sudden souring, not a slow drift.

sugyot.finalRuling: After Shimon HaTzaddik died the era became 'chamtzan' - sour, as the miraculous signs ceased.

display.title: The Year Shimon HaTzaddik Foretold His Death

learning.ahaMoment: Shimon HaTzaddik foresaw his own death; the ominous signs on the Azazel goat confirmed that Yom Kippur's spiritual power was fading.
learning.memoryAnchor: Thin Azazel goat + thread stays red = Yom Kippur atonement weakening; Shimon HaTzaddik knew his time was up.
learning.learnerQuestion: What signs accompanied the specific year Shimon HaTzaddik told his disciples he would die?
learning.coreTension: Shimon HaTzaddik predicted his own death in advance, and that same year the Azazel goat grew thin and the crimson thread did not turn white, raising the question of whether these were independent omens or directly connected to his prophecy.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara places the prediction and the physical signs (thin goat, thread staying red) in the same account, treating the goat's and thread's behavior as confirming evidence alongside his own foreknowledge.

takeaway.text: The year Shimon HaTzaddik foretold his death, the Azazel goat grew thin on its way to the cliff and the crimson thread did not turn white, signs the Gemara reads as confirming that his era of divine favor was ending.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may treat the crimson thread's behavior as a fixed ritual outcome rather than a variable sign whose failure to turn white was itself meaningful.

display.title: Placing the Lots: A Public Oracle

learning.ahaMoment: The lot's hand position was a public divine oracle: right = accepted, left = rejected. Everyone watching knew the verdict.
learning.memoryAnchor: Right hand = God accepts; left hand = God rejects. The lot was a live barometer of national standing.
learning.learnerQuestion: How did the Kohen Gadol designate the two goats after drawing the lots, and what did onlookers learn from it?
learning.coreTension: The lot drawing itself happened in the KG's hands, but its result needed to become public and binding, the question is how the private draw became a visible, formal designation.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara describes the KG placing each lot on the corresponding goat's head and declaring 'chattat l'HaShem,' converting the private draw into a public, verbally confirmed designation that everyone present could witness.

takeaway.text: The KG placed the 'for God' lot on the right goat's head and the 'for Azazel' lot on the left, announcing 'chattat l'HaShem', the lot's outcome was a public, verbally confirmed oracle, not a private determination.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may assume the lot ceremony was a quiet procedural step, missing that the Gemara frames it as a publicly witnessed declaration with real evidentiary weight for the nation.

misconceptions.correction: The lot ceremony was public. When the God-lot came up in the right hand, everyone present could see it. The outcome was a public divine oracle, visible to all.

display.title: Must the God-Lot Land in the Right Hand?

learning.ahaMoment: The miracle of the right-hand lot was a sign, not a requirement - the lot itself designates the goat regardless of hand.
learning.memoryAnchor: Right-hand lot = good omen (sign); but any hand is valid for designation - the miracle was the omen, not the rule.
learning.learnerQuestion: Is it halachically required that the 'for God' lot come up in the Kohen Gadol's right hand, or is this only a good omen?
learning.coreTension: The right-hand lot was celebrated throughout Shimon HaTzaddik's era as a sign of favor, which could suggest it is required for validity, yet the Gemara also describes practical handling for when it lands left, suggesting it remains valid either way.
learning.coreMove: R. Yannai's account of the simultaneous two-handed draw, combined with the description of the Deputy assisting when the lot lands left, leads the Gemara to treat the right hand as the preferred and auspicious outcome, but not the sole valid one.

takeaway.text: Whichever hand draws the 'for God' lot from the box validly designates that goat; the right hand is the favorable omen, but the left hand does not invalidate the ceremony.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may conflate 'good omen' with 'halachic requirement,' missing the Gemara's distinction between what is auspicious and what is strictly necessary for validity.

misconceptions.misconception: The 'for God' lot must come up in the Kohen Gadol's right hand, or the entire designation is invalid.
misconceptions.correction: The Gemara treats the right hand as a favorable omen (siman tov), not a strict requirement for validity. If the lot lands in the left hand, the Deputy helps transfer it and the designation still stands, the right hand's significance is auspicious, not determinative.

rashiTranslations.en: Chometzan - a robber. Give strength to the wronged one - strengthen the one who was robbed. And not the wrongdoer - this is not relevant here;
rather, [in Sanhedrin] (35a), we learn from this that the claimant is addressed first.
From blessing with the Name - from blessing the people with the priestly blessing using the explicit Name, since they were
not worthy of it. Would open on their own - a sign that enemies would come and enter. And already
Zechariah has prophesied against you - that this very opening was itself a sign
of the destruction. Three in the first confession - that of the bull -
'please, the Name, I have sinned; please, the Name, atone,'
'before the Lord shall you be purified.' And one in the lots - 'to the
Lord, a sin-offering.' And he had already said - meaning, there
was once an incident where his voice reached as far as Jericho.
A bride - her practice is to adorn herself with perfumes.
In the hills of Michmar - the name of the district. And I smelled
the fragrance of incense - from the incense that was made there
while the Tabernacle still stood at Shiloh. The rising of the lot
from within the urn is indispensable - for the service, since the goats
are not designated as 'to the Lord' or 'to Azazel' except
by the lot; therefore one must see
which one came up in the right hand, so that the right-hand goat
is designated by it, and which came up in the left, so that the
left-hand goat is designated by it. But
the placing - of the lot upon the goat is not
indispensable, even if he did not place it on the goat, since
the right-hand goat is already established by the lot that came up in the right hand,
and likewise the left-hand goat by the left-hand lot. Even
the rising of the lot is not indispensable - and if the priest calls out
'sin-offering' over one and
'Azazel' over the other, they are established without the lottery,
since the lottery is not indispensable; he has only omitted
a commandment. In accordance with Rabbi Yehuda, etc. -
in the chapter 'They Brought Out for Him' (60a, below), disagree
Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemia, as to one who changed the order of
the services, performing the later one first; and
Rabbi Nechemia says: the entire order of the services performed
in the white garments, whether inside, such as in the innermost sanctum,
or outside, such as in the Sanctuary or the courtyard, is
indispensable, since the statute written in the passage
of 'after the death' [of Aharon's sons] was written concerning them; and Rabbi Yehuda
says the statute is written only regarding matters
performed in the white garments inside; therefore
the lottery, which is performed not inside
but outside - according to Rabbi Yehuda, who says that regarding matters
performed outside, the statute is not written.
That all agree it is not indispensable - since even Rabbi
Yannai concedes that according to Rabbi Yehuda it is not indispensable,
since indispensability is not written regarding them. When
they disagree, it is in accordance with Rabbi Nechemia - who says
the statute applies to all matters performed in the white
garments, and this is performed in the white garments, as is written
in the passage. This applies - where the statute 'chukah' is written
for indispensability regarding a service, it comes for indispensability.
(Up to here, Rabbi Nechemia has only said that 'chukah' is written
for indispensability regarding a genuine service, such as scooping
coals from the altar, or slaughtering the bull,
which are genuine services and are disqualified if performed by another priest;
but the lottery, since it is not a service, is valid
when performed by the deputy - according to the one who said above that the deputy and the High Priest
both insert their right hands into the urn - one might say
that here, even Rabbi Nechemia concedes it is not indispensable.)
All agree it is indispensable -
since it says the statute is written regarding them.
This case is different, since the verse states it explicitly - even
though the statute does not itself stand to render it indispensable,
it is nonetheless indispensable, since the text repeated the requirement
to render it indispensable, and the indispensability is derived from the extra verse.
Rather - the daf ends mid-word here; the comment (resuming the objection's own resolution according to Rabbi Nechemia's view) continues on 40a.
